1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:

NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / No information: No pocket-level or household-level nonresponse rates are reported for the PPSA or baseline KAP surveys, and the discrepancy between the ~65 target SESI slums (PDF p. 7, p. 8) and the 60 open-defecation-free slums / 63 active Community Water and Sanitation Committees reported at project end (PDF p. 10) is not explained.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (uncontrolled): Both the city-wide PPSA survey and the SESI pilot report are purely descriptive with no control/comparison slums or statistical adjustment, making it impossible to separate claimed SESI improvements from concurrent US$400 million ADB city-wide water and sanitation investments or DFID Madhya Pradesh Urban Services Project activities in the same four cities (PDF p. 2, p. 7).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak: While the article centrally distinguishes officially recognised ('notified') slums and Below Poverty Line (BPL) households from 'non-notified slums' omitted from Census and municipal records (PDF p. 3, p. 5, p. 11, p. 13), it cites no statutory or municipal notification criteria, defines no operational verification rule for notification or BPL status, and does not disaggregate Table 1 by legal notification status.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: PPSA quantitative estimates in Table 1 were explicitly 'not a household survey' and relied on key informant interviews and group discussions recorded on questionnaires co-signed by municipal corporation officials and partner NGOs (PDF p. 2, p. 3), creating substantial risk of informant estimation error and institutional desirability bias; SESI outcomes (e.g., 60 open-defecation-free slums, 20,000 families with household toilets, PDF p. 10) are self-reported by an advisor of the implementing agency (UN-HABITAT) without operational definitions or independent verification.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: PPSA water and sanitation access percentages rely on community/informant estimates rather than direct household inspection or water-quality testing, although participatory qualitative inquiry usefully exposes why nominal infrastructure indicators overstate effective access (PDF p. 2, pp. 5-6); SESI intervention outcomes are presented only as rounded administrative output counts and unsubstantiated narrative claims without baseline denominators or independent audit (PDF pp. 10-11).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern: Although the text states that household-level baseline water, sanitation, and hygiene KAP surveys were conducted in selected intervention slums (PDF p. 2, p. 4, p. 8), zero household survey data or pre-post comparisons are reported; furthermore, the data-collection flowchart on PDF p. 4 is missing/blank in the text layer and SESI evaluation findings consist solely of favourable summary outputs reported by a UN-HABITAT Regional Advisor without conflict-of-interest or reflexivity disclosure.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: For the PPSA mapping component, attempting a city-wide census of all notified and non-notified poverty pockets across four cities (1,537 PPs in Table 1, PDF p. 5) reduced administrative exclusion of informal settlements, though operational thresholds for defining a 'poverty pocket' are unreported; selection of the 24 PPs (6 per city) for qualitative participatory exercises and ~65 PPs for the SESI intervention was purposive/consultative with municipal corporations and NGOs without transparent reproducible selection rules (PDF pp. 3-4, 7, 9).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S1: Are there clear research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Although written as an applied UN-HABITAT practitioner report rather than an academic hypothesis-testing paper, the article states clear empirical and operational objectives: to assess water and sanitation deficiencies across all poverty pockets (PPs) in Bhopal, Indore, Gwalior, and Jabalpur to prioritise slums for investment and Municipal Action Plans for Poverty Reduction (MAPP), and to pilot community-led water, sanitation, and hygiene improvements under SESI (PDF pp. 2-3, p. 8).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 2-3 (pp. 580-581, Introduction and Poverty Mapping Framework - Background / Objectives and Strategies); PDF p. 8 (p. 586, SESI - Objectives and Strategies)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S2: Do the collected data allow to address the research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: For the primary poverty-mapping objective, the city-wide PPSA structured survey across 1,537 poverty pockets combined with participatory qualitative fieldwork in 24 poverty pockets provides descriptive quantitative and qualitative data to identify underserved slums and characterize service gaps, even though SESI pilot reporting relies only on uncontrolled administrative output counts.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 2-6 (pp. 580-584, Introduction, Process, Table 1, and Results Achieved); PDF p. 10 (p. 588, SESI - Results Achieved)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.1: Is the qualitative approach appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Using key informant interviews, group discussions, and participatory community exercises is well suited to capturing stakeholder perspectives, seasonal water scarcity, opportunity costs for women and girls, and behavioural/infrastructural reasons for continued open defecation in urban poverty pockets.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF p. 2 (p. 580, Introduction); PDF p. 4 (p. 582, Process); PDF pp. 5-6 (pp. 583-584, Results Achieved)

domain_ratings.justification: While the paper mentions key informant interviews, group discussions, and participatory exercises in six PPs in each of the four cities (24 slums total), it reports no interview/discussion guides, participant numbers or demographics, selection criteria for the six PPs per city, facilitation procedures, or recording/fieldnote protocols.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.3: Are the findings adequately derived from the data?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper summarizes plausible thematic insights (e.g., 4-5 hour summer water-fetching burdens, adolescent girls dropping out of school to fetch water, open defecation persisting among toilet owners due to lack of flushing water and choked drains), but describes no qualitative coding, thematic synthesis method, or analytical process linking raw participatory exercises to reported conclusions.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.4: Is the interpretation of results sufficiently substantiated by data?
domain_ratings.justification: No verbatim participant quotations, participatory matrix outputs, fieldnote excerpts, or slum-specific qualitative case evidence are presented anywhere in the article to substantiate the narrative claims for either the PPSA qualitative survey or the SESI community-empowerment claims.

domain_ratings.justification: Because participant sampling, participatory tool design, and qualitative data analysis methods are not described and primary qualitative evidence is omitted, methodological coherence from data sources through analysis and interpretation cannot be verified.

domain_ratings.justification: Attempting a city-wide enumeration of all notified and non-notified poverty pockets across Bhopal, Indore, Gwalior, and Jabalpur (identifying 1,537 PPs in Table 1) is directly relevant to addressing official Census and municipal under-counting of informal settlements, even though subsequent selection of ~65 SESI intervention slums was purposive/consultative.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.2: Is the sample representative of the target population?
domain_ratings.justification: Although PPSA aimed to map all poverty pockets in the four cities (recording 475,368 households across 1,537 PPs in Table 1), the article provides no operational definition or spatial inclusion threshold for what constituted a 'poverty pocket', does not explain how non-notified pockets were systematically located, and notes that PPSA was not a household survey.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.3: Are the measurements appropriate?
domain_ratings.justification: While MDG water and sanitation indicators are topically relevant, the text explicitly notes that PPSA was not a household survey and relied on key informant interviews and group discussions on forms co-signed by municipal and NGO staff; operational definitions, measurement validation, and verification criteria for Table 1 indicators and SESI 'open defecation free' and household toilet counts are unreported.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.4: Is the risk of nonresponse bias low?
domain_ratings.justification: The article provides no information on pocket-level coverage completeness, key-informant refusals, missing questionnaire items, or response/completion rates for the household-level baseline survey referenced on PDF pp. 2 and 4.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.5: Is the statistical analysis appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Table 1 reports aggregate counts and city-level average percentages without clarifying whether averages are household-weighted or unweighted across PPs, omits measures of dispersion, presents zero quantitative tables from the household KAP baseline survey mentioned in the text, and reports SESI results only as rounded endline output counts without denominators or baseline values.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.1: Is there an adequate rationale for using a mixed methods design to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: The author explicitly justifies combining city-wide quantitative poverty-pocket mapping with participatory qualitative surveys in six PPs per city in order to triangulate quantitative infrastructure numbers and assess service quality, reliability, and lived impacts on slum residents.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.2: Are the different components of the study effectively integrated to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: In the PPSA results narrative, city-level quantitative figures from Table 1 (such as high nominal percentages of improved water sources and sanitation) are directly integrated with participatory qualitative findings explaining seasonal scarcity, crowd pressure per water point, and behavioural/drainage barriers to toilet usage.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 5-6 (pp. 583-584, PPSA - Results Achieved); PDF p. 11 (p. 589, Impact at the strategic/sector level)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.3: Are the outputs of the integration of qualitative and quantitative components adequately interpreted?
domain_ratings.justification: The integrated synthesis meaningfully demonstrates that physical infrastructure counts alone misrepresent effective water and sanitation access in slums when water supply lasts under an hour, summer yields collapse, and inadequate water and drainage choke household latrines, informing holistic intervention design.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 5-6 (pp. 583-584, PPSA - Results Achieved); PDF p. 11 (p. 589, Impact at the strategic/sector level)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.4: Are divergences and inconsistencies between quantitative and qualitative results adequately addressed?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper explicitly highlights and explains the contradiction between high quantitative coverage of 'improved water sources' (66%-96.11%) and personal toilets in Table 1 versus participatory qualitative accounts of 4-5 hour daily summer water collection and continued open defecation due to lack of flushing water and drainage.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.5: Do the different components of the study adhere to the quality criteria of each tradition of the methods involved?
domain_ratings.justification: Neither empirical component satisfies the methodological rigour and reporting standards of its tradition: the qualitative strand omits sampling details, analytical methods, and primary verbatim evidence (1.4 No; 1.2, 1.3, 1.5 Can't tell), while the quantitative descriptive strand relies on unvalidated informant estimates, omits household baseline data and nonresponse details, and reports uncontrolled, unverified programme output counts authored by an implementing-agency advisor (4.2-4.5 Can't tell).

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Singh (2014) is an applied practitioner mixed-methods descriptive mapping and pilot-programme report authored by a UN-HABITAT Regional Advisor examining urban water and sanitation in Bhopal, Indore, Gwalior, and Jabalpur (Madhya Pradesh, India, 2005-2012). Empirically, the first part reports the Poverty Pocket Situation Analysis (PPSA), which combined a city-wide structured community/physical survey across 1,537 notified and non-notified poverty pockets (recording 475,368 households in Table 1) with participatory qualitative surveys in six poverty pockets per city (24 slums total) explicitly designed to triangulate quantitative infrastructure indicators; the second part describes the Slum Environmental Sanitation Initiative (SESI) pilot in ~65 selected slums, reporting uncontrolled end-of-project output counts and narrative lessons learned. Appraised with the MMAT (2018), the study's main strength lies in its mixed-methods rationale and integration (5.1-5.4 Yes): triangulating Table 1 coverage figures with participatory qualitative inquiry effectively reveals both massive official Census under-counting of non-notified slums and sharp divergences between nominal 'improved' water/toilet presence and lived seasonal water scarcity, choked drains, and continued open defecation. However, methodological rigour within each empirical strand is weak (5.5 No): PPSA quantitative figures were derived from key informant interviews and group discussions rather than household enumeration on forms co-signed by municipal and NGO staff without validated definitions or nonresponse reporting (4.2-4.5 Can't tell); qualitative sampling criteria, analytical coding, and verbatim participant evidence are completely absent (1.4 No; 1.2, 1.3, 1.5 Can't tell); promised household baseline KAP survey data are never tabulated; and SESI impacts rely entirely on unverified, uncontrolled output counts reported by an implementing-agency insider amidst concurrent US$400 million ADB and DFID urban water/sanitation investments.
raw_response.overall_rating: High methodological concern / Low overall quality (per MMAT 2018 narrative guidance, no numeric composite score is computed and overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component: mixed-methods triangulation rationale and integration are strong [5.1-5.4 Yes], but both the qualitative strand [1.4 No; 1.2, 1.3, 1.5 Can't tell] and the quantitative descriptive strand [4.2-4.5 Can't tell] have major reporting and measurement deficits, yielding 5.5 No)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Descriptive mixed-methods urban poverty-mapping survey and uncontrolled pilot programme report (combining a city-wide community/key-informant quantitative survey of 1,537 poverty pockets across four cities with participatory qualitative exercises in 24 slums, plus uncontrolled administrative output reporting for a 65-slum water and sanitation pilot)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Introduction and study overview: PDF pp. 1-2 (pp. 579-580); Poverty Mapping Framework (PPSA) background, objectives, NGO/municipal mobilisation, survey/qualitative triangulation process, Table 1, and mixed-methods results: PDF pp. 2-7 (pp. 580-585; note embedded flowchart graphic on PDF p. 4 / p. 582 has no text layer); Slum Environmental Sanitation Initiative (SESI) background, objectives, activities, output counts, strategic impacts, sustainability, and lessons learnt: PDF pp. 7-13 (pp. 585-591).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The paper reports primary empirical data combining a quantitative descriptive component (city-wide structured PPSA questionnaires across 1,537 poverty pockets summarized in Table 1, plus descriptive SESI programme output counts across ~65 slums) and a qualitative component (key informant interviews, group discussions, and separate participatory exercises across six poverty pockets in each of the four cities) with an explicit triangulation rationale (PDF p. 4, p. 582). Because there is no comparator group or quasi-experimental evaluation structure for SESI, ROBINS-I does not apply; instead, MMAT (2018) using the Qualitative (1.1-1.5), Quantitative Descriptive (4.1-4.5), and Mixed-Methods (5.1-5.5) blocks is the exact matching instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
